reader.title: Lynching of Jean Pierre Salet and Didaere
bases: A crowd of armed men took two Black men from their homes and shot them dead for alleged 'incendiary language' (A1, A2, A18).

Every report says a 'crowd' or 'band' of armed men, with no lawful authority mentioned, led two Black men from their homes and killed them with buckshot (A1, A16, A18); the killing was attributed to the men's 'incendiary language', a punishment for speech (A1, A11).

All reports, including the Louisiana papers (A18, A19, A24), trace to Opelousas correspondence of September 17-18 sent to the Picayune and the wire (A1, A2); no independent local or official account was found.

summary.text: The lynching of Jean Pierre Salet and Didaere was the killing of two Black men by a crowd of armed men at Ville Platte Prairie, near Opelousas in St. Landry Parish, Louisiana, on September 16, 1888.
The men were taken from their homes, led a short distance away and shot with buckshot, reportedly because of "incendiary language" they had used.
A short Opelousas dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, under headlines that gave the victims' speech as the cause of their deaths.
The reports came from Opelousas, and a Lake Charles paper headed its reprint "Double Murder in St. Landry."
The papers described the two men only as "negroes" and said the killing was "supposed" to have followed "incendiary language recently used" by them, without saying what the men had said or to whom.

According to an Opelousas special dated September 17 to the New Orleans Picayune, a crowd of armed men rode to the house of the two men at Ville Platte Prairie "yesterday morning," that is, September 16.
After leading them a short distance, the men "riddled them with buckshot, killing both men instantly."
A second wire version, datelined September 18, said the armed men went to the "huts" of the two and took them "to the woods, where they shot them to death."
A Dakota weekly summary added that the band "captured the men" before leading them away and that the victims "were accused of using incendiary language."
The original dispatch closed by noting that the affair "created intense excitement in the neighborhood where it occurred."
No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage, and none of the papers named any of the armed men.
The St. Landry Democrat carried the story only as a copied item in its "Southern Gleanings" column on September 29, nearly two weeks after the killing.
A news brief in the Portland Daily Press was the only report to name the killers' race, saying the two were shot "by white men."
The story reached most readers through the wire, beginning on September 18 in papers such as the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Savannah Morning News and the Indianapolis Journal.

Headlines put the victims' alleged speech at the center: the Globe ran "Negroes of Incendiary Proclivities Killed by a Mob," the Indianapolis Journal "'Incendiary' Negroes Shot to Pieces," and the Morning News "Incendiary Language the Cause of the Shooting."

The Maysville, Kentucky, Evening Bulletin headed its version "Ku-Kluxism With a Variation," while a paragraph elsewhere in the same issue said the men were killed "by a mob who objected to language used by the negroes."
Most papers repeated the dispatch's wording without comment, keeping its hedge that the killing was "supposed" to have been caused by the men's words.
In Louisiana, the Lake Charles Commercial and the St. Martinville Weekly Messenger reprinted the Picayune special, the former under the heading "Double Murder in St. Landry."
The Cleveland Gazette, which described itself as published "in the interest of the Colored People," reprinted the wire item on September 29, credited "Ex.," with "Negroes" capitalized.

The paragraph that followed it, which did not name the case, said that Black Southerners were "compelled to take everything put upon us" and declared that "Violence, intimidation, fraud and murder must cease."

The reports disagree on the day: the original dispatch's "yesterday morning" and the Portland Daily Press's "Sunday" point to September 16, while the Maysville Evening Bulletin said "Monday morning" and a Dakota weekly gave "the 17th."
The September 16 date rests on the earliest dispatch, dated the 17th, which the later versions appear to have recast under new datelines or in weekly summaries.
The second victim's name was printed as Didaere, Sidairo, Didacre and Dideare, and the Maysville paper turned the two names into "Jean Pierre and Salet Dideare."

framing.detail: Northern and Southern dailies ran the wire with headlines naming the victims' speech as the cause: 'Negroes of Incendiary Proclivities Killed by a Mob', 'Shot for Incendiary Language', 'Two Negroes Shot Dead'.
The Maysville Evening Bulletin headed the item 'Ku-Kluxism With a Variation', likening the killing to Klan violence, and the Indianapolis Journal put 'Incendiary' in quotation marks.
Louisiana weeklies reprinted the Picayune special; the Lake Charles Commercial headed it 'Double Murder in St. Landry', and the St. Landry Democrat ran it only as a copied gleaning.
The Black-edited Cleveland Gazette reprinted the item, capitalizing 'Negroes', and followed it with a paragraph saying 'Violence, intimidation, fraud and murder must cease.'
